text: Here’s a Countdown answer. Sixty-six, equals twenty plus seven plus twenty-one plus eighteen.
It adds up. Every number used once. It’s right.
And our checker says... wrong. Zero.
Our own checker. The one we wrote for this course.
What happens next is the most important lesson of the whole capstone. So let’s do one, start to finish.
A worked example. Episode two.
Countdown has been on British TV since 1982. Some numbers, a target, and thirty seconds.
Wait, so where do we get thousands of puzzles?
We make them. Pick four random numbers. Chain them with random operations. If you land on a whole number from one to a hundred, that’s the target.
Otherwise, try again.
We built the answer first, so no puzzle is ever impossible.
Milestone zero: unzip the starter repo, and run the self-test.
It checks every puzzle maker and reward, prints a few sample puzzles, and then: all self-tests passed.
Milestone one: the checker. Think of it as a strict referee.
Only numbers and the four operations. Every number exactly once. No dividing by zero. And hit the target.
And the answer is never run as code. It’s parsed into a tree, and checked piece by piece, with exact fractions.
So nobody can sneak code past it. Safe.
Two rewards are added together.
Neat tags earn half a point. Three of these four replies get that.
Being correct earns a whole point. Only one reply does.
So being right counts twice as much as being tidy.
So, back to our bug. What went wrong?
The checker only looked at the left side of the equals sign. And sixty-six on its own doesn’t use any of the four numbers.
So it’s like reward hacking, but backwards?
Exactly. Reward hacking scores a wrong answer as right. This is the mirror image: a right answer scored as wrong. A false negative.
The lesson for your own task: test correct answers in unusual forms, not only cheating ones.
If we had trained with that bug, what happens to those correct answers?
Pause, and have a guess.
A! Remember episode one? A reward of zero teaches nothing. Nothing moves.
That was before groups. It’s B.
In a group, the other answers score one.
So the group average is high.
And our correct answer, scored zero by the bug, lands below it. Its push is negative.
GRPO would quietly teach the model to stop writing a perfectly good answer.
Wow. A test caught that before any training. That’s why we attack the checker first!
Milestone two: the baseline. Measure the untouched model on two hundred test puzzles, and read ten replies.
Then milestone three, a fifty-step pilot. You only want to know: can learning happen at all?
Is the reward wobbling, but drifting up?
Are there plenty of groups where answers score differently? If they all score the same, there’s no signal.
And are only a few replies being cut off at the length cap?
If the reward is stuck at zero, make it easier. Three numbers instead of four.
Milestone four: three hundred steps. About one to two hours on a free GPU.
And look: groups of eight. No KL leash. A loss with no length bias. Every setting is something you’ve already met.
Oh! I actually know what all of these mean now.
Milestone five: measure again, on the same puzzles, and write it up. These numbers are made up, just to show the shape.
Before and after, side by side. Accuracy, and format. And length too.
And one answer it got wrong?
Always. Make four from these numbers: it wrote something that makes six. Right idea, wrong arithmetic.
One run, one seed, one honest limitation. That’s a strong write-up.
Quick recap.
Build each puzzle from its answer, so none are impossible.
Test your checker with cheats, and with correct answers in odd forms.
And pilot first. Then report before and after, honestly.
Remember where we started? Tiny, getting three plus four wrong.
Then a treat, a nudge, a group, a leash. Rewards it couldn’t fool. Thinking it learned to keep short.
And now we’re training a real model, on a task we picked ourselves.
So pick your task. Measure honestly. And share what you build. We’d love to see it.
You taught a small AI to think.
Thank you so much for learning with us!
See you out there!
